title: Psalms
intro: 46 days through the Psalms, the Bible's book of prayers and songs, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Starting today, 46 days through the Psalms, the book of prayers and songs shared by Jews and Christians. Psalm 1 opens the collection like a gateway, contrasting two ways of life. A person who delights in God's teaching (torah in Hebrew) is pictured as a deep-rooted tree by water: steady, fruitful and green even in dry seasons. The book's 150 poems were collected over centuries into five books, which Jewish tradition compares to the five books of Moses.

Psalm 3 is the first with a heading, linking it to David's flight from his son Absalom (2 Samuel 15); many scholars think such headings were added later. Enemies are many, and they say God will not rescue him. This verse is his answer: God is his shield on every side and the one who restores his honor. In 2 Samuel, David leaves Jerusalem weeping, head covered; "lifts my head" reverses that picture.

A psalm for a clear night. Looking up at the moon and stars, the poet is amazed that the Maker of all that would pay attention to human beings at all. "Son of man" here is a Hebrew way of saying "a human being." The New Testament letter to the Hebrews quotes these lines and reads them in light of Jesus.

posts.display: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?
posts.caption: A lament: a prayer of complaint, often counted as the most common type of psalm. Four times in two verses the poet asks "How long?" Yet in just six verses the psalm moves from protest to trust and even song. The Psalms make room for grief, and even anger at God, inside prayer, something many first-time readers don't expect.

posts.display: The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands.
posts.caption: The psalm's point is that the sky itself speaks: day after day, without words, it points to the God who made it. The second line echoes the first in new words (heavens and skies, declare and proclaim). This is parallelism, the "rhyme" of Hebrew poetry, which rhymes ideas, not sounds. Psalm 19 then moves from the sky's wordless speech to the words of God's law. C.S. Lewis called it "the greatest poem in the Psalter."

posts.display: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning?
posts.caption: A sufferer surrounded by mockers cries out that God has abandoned him, yet still calls him "my God." That tension is the heart of this psalm, which moves from abandonment to praise by its end. These are the words Jesus cries from the cross in Mark and Matthew, and Christians have long read the psalm as foreshadowing the crucifixion; Jewish tradition reads it differently, for example as a prayer of Queen Esther.

posts.display: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name.
posts.caption: The poet pictures God as a shepherd and himself as a sheep in his care: fed, rested, refreshed and guided. The point is complete trust: "I shall not want" means "I lack nothing I need." LORD in capitals marks God's personal name, YHWH, which Jewish readers out of reverence don't pronounce. David, the psalm's traditional author, was a shepherd before he became king, and Psalm 23 is often read at funerals by Jews and Christians alike.

posts.display: The LORD is my light and my salvation—whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life—whom shall I dread?
posts.caption: The poet faces enemies and danger, but begins with confidence: if God is his light and his fortress, there is no one left to fear. Later the psalm pleads with God not to turn away, so trust and anxiety sit side by side. Many Jewish communities recite it daily in the weeks before and through the High Holy Days, a time of reflection and repentance. Its Latin opening, Dominus illuminatio mea, is the motto of the University of Oxford.

A psalm of thanksgiving from someone rescued from the edge of death ("You pulled me up from Sheol," the realm of the dead). The Hebrew verb for "stay the night" is used of a traveler lodging overnight: weeping arrives like an evening guest, but joy comes with the morning. In many communities Psalm 30 is part of the daily Jewish morning service.

In danger, the poet hands his life over to God, trusting God to keep it safe. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus' last words on the cross echo this line: "Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit." Both traditions also pray it at night: Christians at Compline, the last prayer before sleep, and the Jewish hymn Adon Olam ends with an echo of it: "Into His hand I entrust my spirit, when I sleep and when I wake."

The point is a promise: God does not keep his distance from people crushed by grief, but comes close to them. Psalm 34 is an acrostic, its lines beginning with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Its heading recalls David pretending to be insane to escape a Philistine king, and the poem turns that narrow escape into praise. (1 Samuel 21 names the king Achish; the heading's "Abimelech" may be a title for Philistine kings.)

posts.display: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry. He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm.
posts.caption: A song of thanks from someone who waited a long time for help and was rescued. The poet pictures it as being pulled out of a muddy pit and set on solid rock: from sinking despair to firm footing. "I waited patiently" translates a doubled Hebrew verb, literally "waiting, I waited," a way of adding emphasis. The Irish band U2 set this psalm to music as their song "40," which often closed their concerts.

posts.display: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God. My soul thirsts for God, the living God. When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?
posts.caption: The poet, far from Jerusalem and its temple, longs for God the way a thirsty deer longs for water, and aches to worship there again. Book Two of the Psalms begins here, and the heading credits the sons of Korah, a family of Levites who served as temple singers. A refrain repeats, "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" Psalm 43 shares it, so many scholars think the two were once a single poem.

Roaring seas, quaking mountains and warring nations fill this psalm, and then God speaks. "Be still" translates a Hebrew word meaning "let go" or "stop," probably addressed first to the warring nations: stop fighting and recognize who is God. For the worshipers, the point is security: God is with them, a fortress in the chaos. "Selah" may be a musical cue such as a pause. Martin Luther's hymn "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God" is based on this psalm.

The heading sets this psalm after the prophet Nathan confronted David over his sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12). The poet asks for more than pardon: he wants a new heart, something only God can make. "Create" is the Hebrew bara, the verb of Genesis 1, used in the Bible only for God's creating. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles often number most psalms one lower, so this is Psalm 50 there, known by its Latin first word, Miserere.

A lament over betrayal. A few verses later the poet reveals the worst of it: the enemy is not a stranger but "my companion and close friend," someone he once walked with to the house of God. This longing to escape inspired Felix Mendelssohn's anthem "Hear My Prayer," with its famous solo "O for the Wings of a Dove."

The heading sets this psalm in Gath, the Philistine city where David was seized. The poet doesn't claim to be fearless: when fear comes, he chooses to trust, and next to God, human threats shrink. The second verse returns later as a refrain. The psalm also asks God to keep the poet's tears in a bottle, with a Hebrew wordplay: "my wanderings" (nodi) sounds like "bottle" (nod).

posts.display: In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken.
posts.caption: Surrounded by people who bless with their mouths but curse inwardly, the poet finds stability in God alone. The repeated word "alone" is the point: not wealth, status or other people, but God is his rock. In Hebrew, the first line says his soul is "silence" toward God, a quiet, waiting trust. The heading names Jeduthun, one of the musicians who led worship in David's time, and later verses repeat these lines as a refrain.

Psalm 68 is a victory hymn, and many scholars call its Hebrew among the hardest in the Psalms to translate. Amid marching armies and a thundering God, this passage stands out: the God of Sinai is defined by care for orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners. Protecting the fatherless and the widow is a constant theme of the Hebrew Bible's laws and prophets.

One of the few psalms in the voice of an old person. The speaker looks back on trusting God "from my youth" and asks not to be abandoned now that strength is failing, but to live long enough to pass the story on. Its opening lines closely match the start of Psalm 31, one sign that psalms drew on shared words of prayer.

Psalm 72, headed "Of Solomon," prays that the king will defend the poor and bring justice. Book Two of the Psalms closes with these verses, a doxology, or short burst of praise. The point is that the credit belongs to God alone, with a hope that his glory will fill the whole earth. An editor's note follows, "Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse," which many scholars think once ended an earlier collection.

The poet nearly gave up on faith after watching the wicked prosper, until he entered God's sanctuary and saw things differently. These verses are his conclusion: having God is worth more than anything in heaven or on earth, even when body and heart fail. "Portion" recalls the priests, who received no land because, as Numbers 18 says, God himself was their portion. Psalm 73 opens Book Three, the first of eleven psalms in a row credited to Asaph.

A pilgrim's song from the sons of Korah, longing for the temple courts. The point is that one day near God, even in the humblest post, is worth more than a thousand anywhere else. A doorkeeper held a lowly post at the threshold, and 1 Chronicles names Korah's descendants among the temple gatekeepers, which makes the line especially fitting. The psalm's opening, "How lovely is Your dwelling place," became a movement of Brahms' German Requiem.

The psalm prays for God to restore the land after a time of trouble, then pictures the answer. Four great qualities meet like old friends: loving devotion and faithfulness, righteousness and peace (shalom). The point is harmony: when God restores, these blessings arrive together, and heaven and earth meet, as the next verse pictures it. "Loving devotion" is this translation's term for the Hebrew hesed: loyal, committed, covenant love, found more often in the Psalms than in any other book.

Psalm 88 is often called the darkest psalm. Unlike almost every other lament, it never turns to hope or praise, and in Hebrew its very last word is "darkness." The heading credits Heman the Ezrahite. Many readers find it meaningful that a prayer this bleak was kept in the Bible: despair spoken to God is still treated as prayer.

Psalm 89 opens by celebrating God's promise that David's family would rule forever, then ends in shock: the king is defeated and his crown lies in the dust. Here the poet holds God to his own word, asking where that sworn love has gone. Many scholars connect the psalm with the fall of Jerusalem's royal line to Babylon. Book Three closes with this question unanswered, and Book Four opens with a prayer of Moses, from before Israel had kings.

The only psalm credited to Moses, "the man of God." It sets a human lifespan of seventy or eighty years against a God for whom a thousand years are like a single day. This verse draws the lesson: to "number our days" is to count them, knowing they are limited, and the poet asks God to teach that awareness so it leads to wisdom. Isaac Watts' hymn "O God, Our Help in Ages Past" paraphrases this psalm.

A song of protection: whoever makes God their home and shelter is kept safe in his care, like someone resting in his shade. Four names for God appear in these two verses: Most High (Elyon), Almighty (Shaddai), LORD (YHWH) and God (Elohim). Psalm 91 is traditionally prayed at night in both Christian Compline and Jewish bedtime prayers. In Matthew and Luke, the devil quotes it to Jesus during his temptation in the wilderness.

posts.display: It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High, to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night with the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre.
posts.caption: The psalm opens by saying that praising God is simply good, morning and night: thanks for his love at the start of the day and his faithfulness at its end. It's the only psalm whose Hebrew heading names a day: "A song for the Sabbath day." According to the Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, the Levites sang it in the Jerusalem temple on the Sabbath, and it remains part of Jewish Sabbath prayers.

An invitation to worship, as if sung by worshipers approaching the temple: come, sing for joy, and enter God's presence with thanks. God is called "the Rock," an image of strength and safety. Christians know Psalm 95 as the Venite, from its Latin first word ("O come"), and for centuries it has opened daily morning prayer in many churches. In many synagogues it opens Kabbalat Shabbat, the Friday evening service that welcomes the Sabbath.

Psalm 100 is headed "A Psalm of thanksgiving," and it may have been sung as worshipers entered the temple gates. Its last verse gives the reason for all that thanks: God is good, and his love and faithfulness never run out. In English it's famous as the "Old Hundredth," a 16th-century metrical version, "All People That on Earth Do Dwell," whose tune is also sung for the doxology "Praise God, from Whom All Blessings Flow."

The point is how completely God forgives: sins are removed as far as east is from west, two directions that never meet. Psalm 103 is a hymn of thanks for God's mercy, and a few verses earlier it echoes God's description of himself to Moses in Exodus 34: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger." It begins and ends with "Bless the LORD, O my soul," and Psalm 104 opens the same way, so many scholars read them as a pair.

Psalm 104 is a hymn to God as Creator, moving through sky, springs, mountains, animals and sea. Leviathan is a sea monster that ancient Near Eastern myths, and biblical poems like Isaiah 27, use as a symbol of chaos. Here it is simply one of God's creatures, made to play in the sea. Many scholars note parallels between this psalm and an Egyptian hymn to the sun-disk, the Aten.

Book Five opens with thanks from four groups God rescued when they cried out: desert wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors caught in a storm. These verses end the sailors' story: God calms the sea and brings them safely to harbor. For ancient Israel the sea was a symbol of chaos that only God could control, and many readers hear an echo of this passage in the Gospel stories of Jesus calming the storm.

The psalm opens by refusing any credit: the glory belongs to God, because of his love and faithfulness, not to "us." When the nations taunt, "Where is their God?", it answers by mocking idols that "have mouths, but cannot speak." In Latin it begins Non nobis, Domine. In Shakespeare's Henry V, the king orders "Non nobis" sung after the victory at Agincourt, and Kenneth Branagh's 1989 film made that a well-known choral scene.

The shortest psalm, just two verses, and the shortest chapter in the Bible. It calls every nation to praise Israel's God. "Hallelujah" is Hebrew for "Praise Yah," a short form of God's name. Psalm 117 belongs to the Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118), a set of praise psalms sung at Jewish festivals.

A song of thanks for rescue: the stone the builders threw aside has become the cornerstone. The psalm credits God for that reversal and calls it a day to celebrate. Jewish interpreters have often read the stone as Israel or as David; Jesus quotes the line in Mark 12, and early Christians saw in it his rejection and vindication. Psalm 118 closes the Hallel, sung at Passover, which many scholars think Jesus and his disciples sang after the Last Supper.

The point is guidance: God's word is pictured as a lamp lighting the next step on a dark path. Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses in praise of God's teaching. It's an acrostic in 22 stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and all eight lines in each stanza begin with that letter. This verse opens the stanza for nun, and the Hebrew word for lamp, ner, begins with it.

posts.display: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.
posts.caption: Psalms 120 to 134 are each headed "A song of ascents," and many scholars think pilgrims sang them on the way up to Jerusalem, a city in the hills. Looking at the hills ahead, the traveler asks where help will come from, and answers: from the LORD, who made heaven and earth, hills included. The question and answer may have been sung by two voices. Psalm 121 has long been a traveler's prayer, said before journeys.

Psalm 130 begins "Out of the depths I cry to You," known by its Latin opening, De profundis. It is one of the seven Penitential Psalms of Christian tradition, and has long been prayed for the dead. Here waiting for God is compared to night watchmen on a city wall longing for dawn, and the line is repeated, as if the night were long.

posts.display: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in harmony!
posts.caption: Another song of ascents, perhaps sung when pilgrims from many towns gathered in Jerusalem. The point is simply how good it is when people live together in unity, and the psalm reaches for rich images: fragrant anointing oil running down the beard of Aaron, the first high priest, and the dew of Mount Hermon falling on Zion's hills. Its opening words in Hebrew, Hinei ma tov, begin a much-loved Jewish song.

A lament from the exile, after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem around 586 BC and deported many of its people. The next verse asks: "How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?" The psalm ends with a shocking curse on Babylon's children, the raw anger of people who had seen their city destroyed. Its opening became the reggae song "Rivers of Babylon."

Psalm 139 is a meditation on being completely known: God knows the poet's thoughts, path and words before they are spoken, and there is nowhere to escape God's presence. Here the poet traces that knowledge back before birth, picturing God knitting his body together in the womb, and responds with wonder and praise. The psalm ends with an invitation: "Search me, O God, and know my heart."

These verses describe God's character in words that echo Exodus 34, where God passes before Moses: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger and full of loving devotion. The psalm then widens that goodness to all God has made. It is the only psalm headed "A Psalm of praise" (tehillah), and the plural, Tehillim, names the whole book. Observant Jews recite it three times a day, within the Ashrei prayer; the Talmud says whoever does so is assured a share in the world to come.

Psalms 146 to 150 close the book, and each begins and ends with "Hallelujah." This pairing is striking: the God who counts the stars and calls each by name also binds up individual wounds. The psalm speaks of God gathering Israel's exiles and rebuilding Jerusalem, so many scholars date it after the return from Babylon.

The last verse of the Psalms. Psalm 150 calls for praise with horn, harp, lyre, tambourine, dancing and cymbals, then includes every living, breathing thing. The book has traveled from Psalm 1's quiet blessing through grief, anger and thanks to this final "Hallelujah." Jews, and later Christians, have prayed these poems for over two thousand years. Thank you for reading them with me.
